title: Good Leaders Make the Room Smarter
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Contrasts leaders who try to be the smartest person in the room with those who work to raise the room's collective intelligence instead. The argument is that inviting reasoning, not just opinions, is what actually improves decision quality -- prompts like 'walk us through how you got there' shift discussion from viewpoint to rationale. Highlights three specific tactics: deliberately distributing airtime to quieter voices, controlling who speaks first since early framing anchors the discussion, and protecting fragile half-formed ideas long enough for them to develop. The piece frames team discussion as a full-contact sport requiring engagement from everyone, including the leader.
points: Leaders raise decision quality more by requiring and rewarding reasoning ('walk us through how you got there') than by simply soliciting opinions.
Controlling who speaks first matters because the first stated position anchors the discussion; senior voices speaking early collapse the range of ideas that follow.
Protecting a half-baked idea by staying in exploration mode a little longer than expected gives novel insights room to survive.
quotes: Where good leaders invite and reward answers, great leaders require and reward reasoning. They ask everyone to talk out loud about why they believe what they do.

Statements and questions like “Walk us through how you got there,” “What would change your mind?” “Defend that position with evidence,” “What are we presuming?” and “What are we missing?” change the conversation from viewpoint to rationale and from decision to judgment.
When voices are highly distributed, people get less defensive and internal politics lose currency.
They understand that highly experienced or senior voices collapse the breadth of arguments and ideas that others are willing to put forward.
By not letting others brush past it, novel ideas can gain a foothold. If the team doesn’t pick up and run with an insight after the leader hovers over it for a moment, then they move on.
They see team discussions as a full-contact sport where everyone must engage and bring their A-game to the table.
